item.title: U.S. to mediate new round of Ukraine-Russia talks, Witkoff says
item.description:
The U.S. will mediate working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian officials in November, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Tuesday night. In a post on X, Witkoff said the discussions on Nov. 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi would "focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."
He added that American negotiators would meet this week with representatives from European allies and the NATO alliance, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, to discuss future security guarantees for Ukraine, which has been one of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recurring demands for any deal with Russia.
"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg, Russia, Oct. 21, 2026.
Sputnik/Kristina Solovyova/Pool via Reuters
Ukraine and Russia have held several rounds of talks mediated by the U.S. during President Trump's second term, often yielding prisoner exchanges or other low-level agreements, but Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite some controversial concessions from the Trump administration, has thus far refused to drop his demand for Ukraine to accept Russia's unilateral annexation of some territory siezed over the course of the grueling war.
Zelenskyy, likewise, has consistently ruled out accepting Russia's seizure of territory by force, and many U.S. allies in Europe agree that legitimizing Putin's landgrab would set a dangerous precedent.

item.title: Trump says deal with Iran still possible as Americans set to vote
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: American forces launched limited defensive strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News Monday evening. President Trump said on the eve of U.S. midterm elections that a peace deal with Tehran still "could happen," insisting Tehran "wants a settlement, as soon as possible." Mediators continue pushing for a deal to end the eight-month war, but both the U.S. and Iran have publicly stuck to their respective demands.A cargo ship crew member was killed in one of the many recent attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz this week, India's government said Tuesday. Iran has repeatedly warned ships not to use southern routes through the strait that the Trump administration and U.S. military claim are free of mines and open for transit.
New Updates
22m ago
Qatari mediators remain hopeful of deal
Qatar said on Tuesday it remained hopeful that an interim deal could be reached between the United States and Iran as both sides review proposals put forward by mediators.
In recent days, diplomatic efforts have been underway to prevent renewed fighting after the United States threatened major new strikes, though President Trump signalled diplomatic progress with Iran.
"Both parties remain committed to the negotiation process; as we mentioned, we are facilitating the real-time exchange of proposals between them," Qatar's Foreign Ministry Spokesman Majed Al Ansari told reporters.
Both sides "are currently reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented," he added.

item.title: U.S. launches defensive strikes at Iranian targets
item.description:
The U.S. military has launched limited defensive strikes at Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz, three U.S. officials confirmed to CBS News.
A senior U.S. official said the strikes targeted Iran's Qeshm Island after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired at an American aircraft.
The Wall Street Journal first reported on the strikes on Monday.
The strikes came on the eve of Election Day, as President Trump floats restarting hostilities with Iran after the midterms and as the U.S. and Qatari mediators broker talks on a U.S.-Iran deal.
As the war enters its ninth month, Mr. Trump's rhetoric has continued to swing back and forth between striking a deal and launching sustained strikes against Iran again.
In a Truth Social post earlier Monday, the president said a deal "could happen" and that "Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible." Later that night, in an appearance on Fox News, Mr. Trump said "we still have to take care of" several sites in Iran, including Pickaxe Mountain, which houses a suspected nuclear site. During his appearance on Sean Hannity's program, Mr. Trump said it was "not a big deal" and could be done in "an hour."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a weekend call with Mr. Trump, pushed for further sustained strikes against Iran, according to The Associated Press. Mr. Trump acknowledged the call had taken place, saying he had a "very good talk with him," but did not elaborate on what he and Netanyahu discussed.
The war has loomed large over both the U.S. midterm and Israeli parliamentary elections. In the U.S., rising costs stemming from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have led to cratering support for Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.
In Israel, Netanyahu's party lost its majority in the first parliamentary elections since Oct. 7, 2023.
As of mid-October, the Iran war had cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News...

item.title: More European grocery stores hit by apparent fridge-freezer hacks
item.description:
Grocery store chains in at least three European countries reported unexpected temperature spikes Monday in refrigerators and freezers that ruined food — the second time in less than a month that similar incidents have raised concerns about cyberattacks on increasingly interlinked infrastructure.
Netherlands-based food retailer Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt in Belgium both said an IT incident overnight had sent temperatures inside fridges and freezers in dozens of their stores in Belgium and Luxembourg soaring, while Swedish chains ICA and Coop reported similar spikes, with one outlet explicitly blaming a cyberattack, according to the Reuters news agency.
The incidents come less than three weeks after several French supermarket chains said they were hit by a cyberattack that sent refrigerator temperatures surging as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit in hundreds of outlets.
French chains E. Leclerc, Intermarché and Cooperative U told the AFP news agency last month that they had suffered a cyberattack.
On Monday, Reuters said Ahold, the Dutch grocery store chain, had reported a cybersecurity incident to police in the Netherlands in October after detecting suspicious activity in its infrastructure. The chain realized there were temperature increases in the cooling systems on Monday, Delhaize spokesperson Sarah De Meester told Reuters.
The CEO of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates the systems used by Delhaize and other chains, told Belgium's national Belga news agency a cyberattack was to blame after fridge and freezer units' evaporators were switched into defrost mode.
"We began mobilizing technicians at 1 a.m. to get the situation under control," Stephan Moelans told Belga. "We've been working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network."

item.title: Hacked alert apps send Ukrainians, Russians fake attack warnings
item.description:
Kyiv — Ukrainian and Russian emergency alert apps used to warn civilians of incoming missiles, drones and other military attacks were hacked hours apart on Sunday night, sending out false messages about radiation, chemical attacks and nuclear strikes.
At 10:47 p.m. local time (3 p.m. Eastern), Air Alert, a Ukrainian app developed by Ajax Systems and Stfalcon with support from Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation, started sending out false warnings of radiation, chemical threats, a nuclear attack and even street fighting in Kyiv.
Some Ukrainians rely on the app to decide whether or not to take shelter ahead of incoming Russian missile and drone strikes. Many also rely on the social media platform Telegram, however, where the country's Air Force and security analysts share more specific information about incoming strikes.
The Ukrainian Air Force confirmed just 10 minutes later, at 11:02 p.m. local time, on multiple platforms, that the notifications were false. "The Air Alert app appears to have been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat!" the Air Force said in a message shared on Telegram, urging Ukrainians to remain calm and follow official updates.
A smartphone displays notifications from the emergency alert app "Air Alert" in Kyiv, Ukraine, received on the evening of Nov. 1, 2026, amid Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine. The notifications, sent due to a hack of the app, reached millions of people across Ukraine, warning of a "nuclear alert," a "chemical threat" and even "street fights" in Kyiv.
Roman PILIPEY/AFP/Getty
Some Kyiv residents told CBS News they immediately knew the notifications were fake after checking Telegram channels.

item.title: U.K. man returns home after 28 years walking 30,000 miles around the world
item.description:
Hull, England - For 28 years and one day, Karl Bushby took the long way home on an epic odyssey of human endurance back to northern England.
His adventure was made even more difficult - physically and mentally - with his two self-imposed guiding rules: he could not advance his journey with the help of any machine and he could not return home during the entire time, even if family or friends died.
It was also hardly a direct route. His journey was delayed at various times for months, if not years, by illness, visa restrictions in Russia, Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and having to swim massive bodies of water. His life was also threatened by armed gangs in the lawless Darien Gap in Central America, jail in Panama and a polar bear in Siberia.
Karl Bushby crossing North Bridge as he arrives back home in Hull, England, following his 28-year walk from Chile.
Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA Images via Getty Images
Starting out at 29, he sported golden locks in his earliest pictures. Now 57, his beard is salt-and-pepper, and the elements and time weather his face.
On Monday, he took his final steps of an estimated 75 million to a hometown hero's welcome of claps and cheers as he walked into Hull, a gritty and proud working-class port city.
"I didn't do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team: Earth. That's what it took to get me back," said Bushby to the assembled well-wishers in Hull, a working-class port city about 150 miles north of London.
"You wouldn't believe just how many people have been involved in this, to get us around the kinds of obstacles that we faced. We faced down governments. We faced down some of the hardest challenges. item.title: Record bounty offered for fugitive drug kingpin "Chubby Jos"
item.description:
Dutch authorities are offering a record reward of 2 million euros ($2.2 million) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe's most-wanted drug traffickers, currently hiding in Sierra Leone.
The arrest of Leijdekkers, also known as "Bolle Jos" ("Chubby Jos"), is "the highest priority for the Public Prosecution Service and the police," said Dutch prosecutors in a statement, multiplying by 10 their previous reward.
Leijdekkers is considered to be one of the key players in the international cocaine trade.
A court in Rotterdam sentenced him in absentia in 2024 to 24 years in prison for drug shipments totaling nearly 7,000 kilos of cocaine, an armed robbery, and ordering a "liquidation."
He has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.
Dutch police have tracked the 35-year-old to Sierra Leone. Any information shared with prosecutors will be kept secret, the Dutch authorities said in a statement.
Jos Leijdekkers, aka "Chubby Jos."
Europol
Justice Minister David van Weel said the increase in the reward was "necessary given the threat that Leijdekkers poses to national security, our democratic rule of law, and the international legal order."
"The Netherlands, in cooperation with the international community, is doing everything in its power to secure the arrest of Leijdekkers," the minister said in a letter to parliament.
Links to Sierra Leone
In January 2025, Dutch authorities said they were "absolutely certain" he was hiding out in Sierra Leone. The BBC reported that Dutch prosecutor Wim de Bruin said the fugitive's return to the Netherlands was of "the highest priority."

item.title: Italy revels in 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli's Formula 1 supremacy
item.description:
Rome — In the Italian town where Kimi Antonelli grew up, the celebrations were well underway Monday, even before the new Formula One World Champion's friends, family and neighbors knew when he might come back home to join them.
More than 500 people had gathered Sunday at a theater in Casalecchio to watch their hometown driver clinch the title in Mexico, the town's mayor told Italian news agency ANSA. A proper welcome awaits as soon as his racing schedule allows him to come home.
Antonelli became the youngest world champ in Formula One history on Sunday and the first Italian to claim the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.
Team Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli of Italy celebrates being crowned the Formula One World Champion at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez in Mexico City, Mexico, Nov. 1, 2026.
Francisco Canedo/Xinhua/Getty
Max Verstappen won the race, but Antonelli's third-place finish in the Mexico City Grand Prix was more than enough to secure him the championship in overall season ranking.
Pride quickly swelled beyond Casalecchio, which is near Bologna. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni hailed the 20-year-old as a source of national pride, while Italian tennis star Jannik Sinner joined other big names in sports to congratulate the young racer with social media posts.
While Italian F1 racing is synonymous with the Ferrari brand, its new champion drives for Mercedes. He shared Sunday's podium with Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, the seven-time champion he replaced on the Mercedes team.
